idiom_name: rebuild the container and rebind (a = a.first(n) / a.slice(0, n); String#byteslice)
implementation_notes: Ruby's Array and String expose no capacity at all - the interpreter allocates the backing store, and the class documents element operations only - so there is nothing to trim in place and the pattern is hand-written: finish the shrink phase, then replace the object with a right-sized copy built from the survivors (a = a.first(n), a = a.slice(0, n), a = Array.new(a); strings via s = s[0, n] or s.byteslice(0, n)). MRI copies into the requested size and the previous buffer becomes garbage, so the operation is really 'replace, then let the garbage collector collect'; Object#dup is not a trim (it copies the current length and inherits the interpreter's storage decision), and Object#clone differs from dup by keeping frozen state and the singleton class. In-place element removal (slice!, delete_if, clear) keeps identity but leaves storage reclamation entirely to the interpreter.
code_sketch:
rows = payload.map { |line| parse(line) }   # peak ~250k rows
rows = rows.select(&:keep)                  # new, right-sized Array; old one is garbage
# identity must survive (element-level only):
# rows.slice!(n..)                          # or rows.delete_if { |r| r.stale }
# strings: s = s.byteslice(0, n)
pitfalls: Rebinding leaves the old container alive for every other holder (instance variable, closure, another collection): memory is released only when the last reference goes away, so the trim is easy to defeat silently.
Array#dup/#clone are not trims - they copy the current length and inherit the interpreter's storage sizing; only building from a slice/first(n) gives a right-sized result.

In-place slice!/delete_if change elements without any capacity promise (MRI decides when to reallocate), and frozen objects raise FrozenError, so 'trim by mutation' is not available on a frozen literal.
sources: docs.ruby-lang.org, class Array (Ruby 3.3) - the documented interface is element/value operations (access, adding, removing, destructive selection via select!/reject!/delete_if/keep_if, compact/uniq); no capacity, trim or shrink operation is documented: https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/3.3/Array.html
